title: Mission Tiles
description:
Mission tile roofing, also known as “Monk and Nun”, consists of two rows of arched tiles laid on top of each other - the top row with the convex side facing up and the bottom row with the convex side facing down.
Mission tiled roofs will sometimes have the edges filled in with plaster.

title: Spanish Tiles
description:
While seemingly similar to mission tiles, a spanish tile roofing consists of single tiles with a flat part and an arch, rather than two separate arched tiles. The flat part is bent on the edge opposite to the arch, which helps connect neighbouring tiles together
When looking from afar, the “arches” are usually visibly more spaced than in a mission tile roofing. The gap separating the tiles will also be visible only on one side (almost always right) of the arched segment, which is helpful for when the roof edge is obscured. In contrast, mission tile roofs will have the gap visible on both sides of the top tiles, since they are not connected.

title: Maranhão tiles
description: A variant of the mission tile roofing, where both the bottom and the top tiles are characterized by a trapezoidal profile, rather than an arched one. They are also known as “Maranhão tiles”.

title: Flat Mission Tiles
description: A variant of the mission tile roofing, where both the bottom and the top tiles have a visibly flatter profile.

title: Flat Spanish Tiles
description:
A variant of the spanish tile roofing, where the “arched” end of the tiles have a visibly flatter profile. Similarly to spanish tiles, this type of roofing consists of single tiles with a flat part and a flattened arch.
As opposed to flat mission tiles, the gap separating the tiles will be visible only on one side (almost always right) of the arched segment.

title: Marseille Tiles
description: Marseille tile roofing consists of short segments of corrugated ceramic or concrete tiles with multiple irregular protrusions per tile.

title: Corrugated Fibre Cement
description: Corrugated roofing sheets, usually gray in color, but can rarely be painted. They are often mistaken for metal sheet roofs, but are in fact made out of fibre cement, which is manifested by the fact that instead of rusting, these sheets become darker over time.

title: Lamp head built in two visible parts
description: Street lamp whose head is made of two distinct parts, one behind the other. Most common in Minas Gerais and Goiás; also reaches Rio Grande do Sul in the south and Rio Grande do Norte in the north, and spills from Goiás into the Federal District. Extremely rare in Pará, Mato Grosso and Rondônia.

title: Off-centre crossbeam with a long support bar
description: Pole top whose crossbeam and insulators sit off-centre, with a diagonal support bar running up to the middle of the longer arm. Extremely common in São Paulo state, common in Rio Grande do Sul, uncommon in Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo and Mato Grosso do Sul (especially around Três Lagoas), rare in Mato Grosso.

title: Gamma pole with a box at the end of the crossbeam
description: Gamma-shaped pole carrying an electricity box out at the end of its crossbeam. Most common in Belém, Salvador and Rio de Janeiro.

title: Gamma pole with a short crossbeam and a box
description: Version of the gamma pole whose crossbeam is noticeably shorter, with the electricity box on it. Only seen in Belém.

title: Electricity meters in a cabinet on the pole
description: Several electricity meters grouped in a glazed cabinet bolted straight onto the utility pole. Most common in Mato Grosso, Pará and Amapá; a more compact version turns up in Paraíba.

title: Pole tapering to a blunt point
description: Concrete pole whose top narrows to a blunt point, like a sharpened pencil. Most common in Rio de Janeiro, also found in Manaus and in the Federal District.

title: Small yellow plate set flush into the pole
description: Yellow identification plate embedded flush into the concrete of the pole, used by CEMAR, the Maranhão electricity utility. Spills into Pará and Piauí.

title: CEMAR moulded down the pole
description: The utility name CEMAR cast vertically into the concrete of the pole — Maranhão. Utility names are commonly moulded into Brazilian poles, and they often echo the name of the state.

title: Yellow band plate, one letter then digits
description: Yellow identification plate wrapped around the pole, carrying a single letter followed by digits. Used state-wide by CELPA, the Pará utility.

title: Flat crossbeam with no diagonal struts
description: Pole top with a flat, off-centre crossbeam carrying its insulators and no diagonal support struts, on a mast pierced with small holes. Used state-wide in Ceará by COELCE.

title: Yellow plate held on by a zip tie or a metal strap
description: Yellow identification plate fastened to the pole with a zip tie or a thin metal strap, used by COSERN in Rio Grande do Norte. The same plate shows up rarely in Pernambuco, but mounted much higher up the pole.

title: Orange-yellow painted band with black characters
description: Band painted around the pole in orange-yellow, carrying black characters that begin with a letter, often with COELBA written down one side. Bahia. Pernambuco paints its poles almost identically, so other local details are needed to separate the two.

title: Squat insulators on a bare flat crossbeam
description: Plain flat crossbeam fitted with these particular squat insulators, used here and there in Bahia.

title: COELBA moulded down the pole
description: The utility name COELBA cast vertically into the concrete of the pole — Bahia.

title: CELPE moulded down the pole
description: The utility name CELPE cast vertically into the concrete of the pole — Pernambuco.

title: Yellow painted band, one letter then digits, on a tall pole
description: Band painted yellow down the pole with black characters starting with a letter. The Pernambuco pattern, near-identical to Bahia's, so look for the state's other pole details to separate them. This one is from Serra Talhada.

title: Square yellow painted patch with black characters
description: Identification painted as a squared-off yellow patch rather than a band around the pole. Seen in Santa Cruz do Capibaribe, Pernambuco.

title: Small yellow plate mounted high up the pole
description: The plate Rio Grande do Norte uses, but fixed much higher up the pole than there — a Pernambuco habit.

title: Brown mushroom-shaped insulators
description: Crossbeam carrying brown insulators shaped like mushroom caps. A Pernambuco feature, and one of the details that separates it from Bahia, whose pole paint is nearly the same.

title: Lamp head with a brightly coloured tip
description: Alagoas street lamps come in a range of head colours, the tip being what catches the eye from the road.

title: Black plate with yellow digits read vertically
description: Goiás identifies its poles either with yellow paint and black digits, or with a black plate carrying yellow digits like this one. Both are found across the state, Goiânia included.

title: Elongated blue lamp head
description: Long, flat lamp head painted blue, the lens panels visible from underneath. Tocantins.

title: Salmon-orange lamp head with a blue cap
description: Rounded lamp head in salmon-orange with a small blue fitting on top. Belém.

title: Long vertical number on a yellow painted band
description: Pole carrying a long string of digits read vertically on a painted band. Belém has a great many rare pole identifications of this kind.

title: Red-orange lamp head on a curved arm
description: Compact lamp head in red-orange. Boa Vista uses this one; the same fitting turns up in other Roraima towns in different colours — blue in Rorainópolis, yellow in Caracaraí, green in Pacaraima.

title: Kerbs painted in black and white stripes
description: Kerbstones painted in alternating black and white bands along the street. Boa Vista.

title: Piles of earth left in wide unpaved streets
description: Heaps of sand or earth left standing in the street, alongside unusually wide roadways. Boa Vista.

title: Yellow plate with widely spaced digits
description: Pole identification on a yellow plate, the digits spread well apart. Boa Vista.

title: Pair of white meter boxes bolted to the pole
description: Two white electricity meter boxes fixed one above the other on the pole. Possible in Macapá.

title: White PMM plate with a dotted number
description: Small white plate reading PMM above a number written with a full stop as separator. Macapá.

title: Flat dark lamp head with a blue cap
description: Slim, flat lamp head in dark grey with a small blue fitting on top. Macapá.

title: Dark green rounded lamp head
description: Rounded lamp head painted dark green. Unique to Manaus but not common there.

title: Pole identification above the lamp arm
description: In Manaus the identification plate is usually fixed above the lamp arm rather than at eye level.

title: Corroded sign with a large number and letter
description: Street sign in green and white carrying a big number and letter, every one of them corroded. Palmas.

title: CELTINS moulded down the pole
description: The utility name CELTINS cast vertically into the concrete of the pole. Tocantins utility names are unusually legible on the poles.

title: PREMOLTINS moulded down the pole
description: The name PREMOLTINS cast vertically into the concrete of the pole. Tocantins.

title: Wide empty flat roads with roundabouts
description: Roads that are wide, almost empty, laid out oddly and perfectly flat, with roundabouts. Palmas.

title: Square concrete litter bin on a post
description: Litter bin cast in concrete, square and mounted on a single post. Porto Velho.

title: Yellow plate, one letter then four digits
description: Pole identification on a small yellow plate, a letter followed by four digits. Porto Velho.

title: Hazy sky over the street
description: A hazy, washed-out sky is common in Porto Velho.

title: Roadway paved in red-pink bricks
description: Road surface laid in small red-pink bricks. Rio Branco.

title: White concrete LIXO bin on a post
description: Litter bin in white concrete on a single post, with LIXO cast into the side. Rio Branco.

title: Blue street plate laid flat against the pole
description: Street-name plate in blue, fixed flat against the pole rather than standing out from it. Rio Branco.

title: Timber houses raised on stilts
description: Houses built of timber, some raised on stilts, behind wooden fences. Rio Branco.

title: Chrome lamp head with a pointed front and a coloured top
description: Polished, almost mirror-bright lamp head whose front comes to a point, with a blue or yellow light on top. São Luís.

title: Small white plate with a spaced number
description: Pole plate in white carrying a number split by a space. Specific to São Luís.

title: Identification band on the lamp arm
description: Common spoon-shaped lamp head, but with an identification band wrapped around the arm that carries it. Aracaju.

title: Large blue street sign with the postcode on it
description: Street-name sign on a big blue panel, with the neighbourhood and the CEP postcode printed along the bottom. Aracaju, where the utility is SIGMA.

title: Pole top held together with zip ties
description: Sometimes the identification is unreadable and only the zip ties holding it are visible. Aracaju.

title: Smooth tapered lamp head
description: Lamp head with a smooth, aerodynamic taper and no visible seams. Fortaleza.

title: Red sticker on the lamp head
description: Small red sticker stuck to the side of the lamp head. Unique to Fortaleza.

title: Digits painted straight down the pole
description: Identification painted directly onto the concrete, read from top to bottom. Fortaleza.

title: Sidewalks and driveways of irregular stone
description: Pavements and driveways laid in irregular flat stones. Very common in João Pessoa, along with plain white dashed road lines; a yellow dash is rare there.

title: Ladder pole with unusually many openings
description: Ladder-type concrete pole pierced with more openings than usual. More common in João Pessoa than in other cities.

title: Narrow yellow plate with four digits
description: Pole identification on a narrow yellow plate carrying four digits. Uncommon, and roughly state-wide in Paraíba.

title: Small white plate, one letter then five digits
description: Pole identification on a small white plate, a letter followed by five digits. Maceió.

title: Green street sign with the postcode on it
description: Street-name sign on a green panel with the CEP postcode along the bottom. Maceió, where a blue version also exists.

title: Long arm with a bend at the top and a coloured underside
description: Tall pole whose lamp arm bends near the top, the lamp head showing a yellow or grey spot underneath. Maceió.

title: Orange plate with five digits
description: Pole identification on an orange plate carrying five digits. Rare, Maceió.

title: Yellow plate, one letter then two digits, on a strap
description: Small yellow plate held to the pole by a thin strap, carrying a letter and two digits. Natal, and across all of Rio Grande do Norte.

title: Internet offer posters stuck on the poles
description: Poles papered with printed offers for home internet, price and phone number in large type. Very common in Natal.

title: Yellow painted band, one top letter then digits
description: Band painted down the pole with a letter above the digits. Within Recife the letter can be R, H, E or B; the same paint is used across Pernambuco.

title: Blue RECIFE panel on a post
description: Blue panel carrying the name RECIFE on a slim post. Often faded, so the shape is what to go by.

title: Cream bollard with black bands
description: Short bollard painted cream with black bands around it. Very common in Salvador, sometimes yellow and black instead.

title: Long yellow sticker along the lamp arm
description: Identification on a long yellow sticker running along the lamp arm. Salvador.

title: Poles papered with EMPRÉSTIMO loan adverts
description: Poles covered in printed adverts offering consumer loans, EMPRÉSTIMO in large type with a phone number. Salvador.

title: Black and white mosaic pavement in a wave pattern
description: Pavement of small black and white stones laid in a curling wave pattern. Salvador, which also uses other broken-tile patterns in the same two colours.

title: Thin horizontal white plate
description: Pole identification on a thin white plate mounted horizontally, digits in a single row. Teresina.

title: Crossbeam meeting the pole at a right angle
description: Pole top whose top bar sits square to the pole. Common in Brasília.

title: Yellow dashed centre line with speed bumps
description: Roads marked with a yellow dashed centre line and fitted with speed bumps. Very common in Brasília.

title: Blue and green sign giving a block reference
description: Address sign in blue over green giving a block reference and the buildings it covers, rather than a street name. Brasília.

title: Wide avenue with no poles and curved lamp posts
description: Streets that suspiciously lack utility poles, lit instead by their own curved lamp posts. Brasília.

title: Neon-yellow sticker read vertically
description: Pole identification on a narrow neon-yellow sticker read from top to bottom. Campo Grande, and state-wide in Mato Grosso do Sul. Vitória uses a similar one.

title: Blue street sign wrapped around the pole
description: Street-name sign printed on a blue sheet wrapped right around the pole, with the postcode at the bottom. Campo Grande, and state-wide in Mato Grosso do Sul.

title: Lamp head with a green shell
description: Rounded lamp head whose shell is painted green. Cuiabá — not to be confused with the green lamps of Manaus or Vitória.

title: Six or more meter boxes stacked on one pole
description: Electricity meter boxes grouped in banks on a single pole. Seen in other cities too, but in Cuiabá there are usually three to six of them, often more.

title: Two-part lamp head with the pole visible beneath
description: Lamp head in two parts, mounted so the top of the pole stays visible underneath. Goiânia, and across Goiás.

title: White plate on a bracket, number starting 0 or 1
description: Pole identification on a white plate held out on a small bracket. In Belo Horizonte the number starts with 0 or 1; in Uberaba it starts with 2.

title: Pole built as a tall frame with two horizontal bars
description: Utility pole made up as a tall metal frame carrying two long horizontal bars. When something out of the ordinary is happening with the pole, it tends to be Rio de Janeiro.

title: Curving lamp arm with a large head
description: Lamp arm that curves in a long sweep, usually ending in a large head. Rio de Janeiro.

title: Large white box high on the pole
description: Big white box mounted high on the pole among a tangle of cabling. Spammed in São Gonçalo and found across Rio de Janeiro state.

title: Yellow taxis
description: Taxis in Rio de Janeiro are yellow.

title: Long straight lamp neck with a tight bend at the top
description: Lamp arm running straight and long before turning through a tight bend at the top, usually ending in a thin head. São Paulo city.

title: Painted band on the pole reading SP
description: Painted band whose identification includes the letters SP. São Paulo.

title: Black plate with neon-yellow digits read vertically
description: Pole identification on a black plate with neon-yellow digits, mounted vertically. Vitória — São Paulo's neon-yellow one usually runs the other way.

title: Blue street sign with a green stripe and a red postcode bar
description: Street-name sign in blue with a green stripe under the name and the CEP postcode on a red bar. Vitória.

title: Red tactile paving of small studded tiles
description: Tactile paving in red, made of small tiles covered in circular studs, laid along the kerb. Very common in Vitória.

title: Lamp head with a green shell and a blue cap
description: Rounded lamp head with a green shell and a small blue fitting on top. Vitória — not to be confused with the green lamps of Manaus or Cuiabá.

title: Metal box wedged between plastic meter boxes
description: Bank of electricity meters where a metal box sits sandwiched between the plastic ones. Very common in Vitória.

title: Blue plate with a short mixed code on the lamp arm
description: Small blue plate on the lamp arm carrying a short code of letters and digits with a dash. Curitiba.

title: Blue sign read vertically on the pole
description: Street sign on a blue panel read from top to bottom, fixed to the pole. Curitiba, which also still uses the ordinary sign.

title: Paved footway set behind a grass verge
description: Footway of small pavers separated from the roadway by a strip of grass, the road edged with a yellow outer line. Common in Curitiba.

title: Araucária, the candelabra-shaped pine
description: Araucária pine, its branches held out flat in a candelabra shape. Curitiba and the Paraná highlands.

title: Pole banded in red, white and blue near the top
description: Pole painted with red, white and blue bands near the top. Florianópolis, where the same banding turns up on signposts.

title: Roadway paved in hexagonal blocks
description: Road surface laid in interlocking hexagonal blocks. Not unique, but very common on residential roads in Florianópolis.

title: Blue street sign with a council crest and the state code
description: Street-name sign in blue carrying the council crest, the postcode, the neighbourhood and the state code. Florianópolis and São José.

title: Red lamp head
description: Rounded lamp head painted red, the Belém fitting, spammed across one neighbourhood of Florianópolis.

title: Leafy, roomy residential streets
description: Streets noticeably greener, cleaner and roomier than in any other Brazilian city, which makes the common wooden poles look out of place. Porto Alegre.

title: Yellow plate with six digits on a strap
description: Pole identification on a yellow plate carrying six digits. Porto Alegre.

title: Pavement of large square slabs
description: Footway laid in large plain square slabs. Used across Rio Grande do Sul and spilling into Santa Catarina.

title: Yellow band with a three-letter town code
description: Band painted yellow on the pole carrying a three-letter abbreviation of the town above the digits — GUL, BAR, SPU, ITP, SBC and others. Greater São Paulo.

title: Signposts painted red
description: Posts carrying road signs painted red rather than grey. Various towns in São Paulo state.

title: Wave-patterned mosaic pavement, sometimes with birds
description: Pavement of small black and white stones in a wave pattern, occasionally worked into bird figures. Campinas.

title: Street name painted down the pole with colour bands
description: The street name applied directly to the pole, read from top to bottom, usually with coloured bands above and below. Paraná, where metal signs are dear. Possible on ladder poles in northern Rio Grande do Sul.

title: Black painted panel with yellow digits
description: Panel painted black down the pole carrying yellow digits, sometimes with an arrow beneath. Paraná, but not in Curitiba, so not quite state-wide.

title: Small black painted square on the pole
description: A single small square painted black on the pole. Rare in Paraná, and usually on one of the larger poles.

title: Ornate white urn-shaped lantern on a plain pole
description: Decorative lantern with a white urn-shaped globe, bracketed onto an ordinary concrete pole. Several towns in Paraná.

title: Undersized lamp head on a very short bracket
description: Small lamp head fixed to the pole on a stub of a bracket, far shorter than the usual arm. Several towns in Paraná.

title: Yellow painted identification starting with L
description: Identification painted in yellow down the pole, opening with the letter L above the digits. Londrina.

title: Number written on the pole by hand in blue
description: A number daubed on the pole by hand in blue paint. Londrina.

title: Number written on the pole by hand in white
description: A number daubed on the pole by hand in white paint. Cascavel.

title: Amber lamp head shaped like a spoon
description: Lamp head in amber, its bowl shaped like the back of a spoon. Cascavel.

title: Blue lamp head
description: Rounded lamp head painted blue. Santarém, Pará.

title: Meter cabinet left open or wrecked
description: Electricity meter cabinet on the pole, hanging open or broken up. Towns in Pará outside Belém.

title: Meter boxes with yellow skull hazard stickers
description: Column of electricity meter boxes up the pole, each carrying a yellow hazard sticker with a skull. Common in Marabá, Pará.

title: Yellow plate notched on both sides
description: Identification plate in yellow with a semicircular notch cut into each side. Imperatriz, Maranhão.

title: Long tapered lamp arm with a fin
description: Ornate lamp whose long arm tapers into a fin below the head. Imperatriz, Maranhão.

title: Very small amber lamp head
description: An unusually small amber lamp head on a plain bent arm. Gurupi, Tocantins.

title: Oversized yellow plate along the lamp arm
description: Identification on a very long yellow plate running along the lamp arm. Betim, Minas Gerais.

title: White plate with a number starting 2 or 3
description: Pole identification on a white plate whose number usually starts with 2 or 3. Uberaba, and among Minas Gerais cities only Belo Horizonte and Uberaba use this plate.

title: Road markings painted on stone setts
description: Painted lane markings applied directly onto a roadway of stone setts. Caxias do Sul — the only place the guide's authors have seen stone carry markings.

title: Blue street name painted down the pole
description: Street name applied in blue directly down the pole. Sinop, Mato Grosso.

title: Long white swan-neck lamp arm
description: Lamp arm in white sweeping up and over in a long swan neck. Barra do Garças, Mato Grosso.

title: Ônitel internet posters on the poles
description: Poles carrying blue printed adverts for Ônitel home internet, with the speed, the price and a phone number. Luziânia, Goiás.

title: Dark red lamp head with a coloured cap
description: Rounded lamp head in dark red with a small coloured fitting on top. Itumbiara, Goiás.

title: Flat lamp head with a box on top
description: Slim flat lamp head carrying a small box on its upper side, on a bent arm. Joinville, Santa Catarina.

title: Blue street plate read vertically with Rua spelled out
description: Street-name plate in blue read from top to bottom, opening with Rua and a colon. Joinville, Santa Catarina.

title: Ladder pole with a two-strut crossbeam
description: Slotted concrete pole — the ladder profile, a long groove and a line of holes down its face — carrying a crossbeam braced by two diagonal struts. Surveyed share: Amapá 96%, Acre 95%, Amazonas 85%, Goiás 78%, Mato Grosso do Sul 73%, Tocantins, Mato Grosso and Paraná 71%, Pará 65%, Bahia 51%, Rondônia 47%, Rio Grande do Sul 35%. Never recorded in Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba, Sergipe or Ceará, where the poles carry no struts at all.

title: Ladder pole with one long diagonal brace
description: Slotted ladder-profile pole whose crossbeam is held by a single strut running a long way down the pole. Surveyed share: Rio de Janeiro 19%, Espírito Santo 14%, Rio Grande do Sul 12%, Mato Grosso 10%, then under 10% in São Paulo, Bahia, Paraná, Pará, Paraíba, Mato Grosso do Sul, Pernambuco, Amazonas and Minas Gerais. Absent from the North-East and the far North.

title: Ladder pole with one short diagonal brace
description: Slotted ladder-profile pole whose crossbeam is held by a single short strut, meeting the pole just below the beam. Surveyed share: Santa Catarina 36%, Tocantins 29%, Minas Gerais 10%, then under 10% in Mato Grosso, Espírito Santo, Acre, Goiás, Paraíba, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo and Paraná.

title: Ladder pole braced from behind
description: Slotted ladder-profile pole whose single strut is fixed on the far side of the pole instead of under the beam, so it appears to lean away from the road. Recorded only in Santa Catarina (9%) and Minas Gerais (8%).

title: Round pole with a two-strut crossbeam
description: Plain cylindrical concrete pole carrying a crossbeam braced by two diagonal struts that form a V beneath it. Surveyed share: Rio de Janeiro 39%, Espírito Santo 38%, Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul 27%, São Paulo 22%, Goiás 18%, Mato Grosso do Sul 16%, Santa Catarina 14%, Roraima 10%. Absent from the whole North-East.

title: Round pole with one long diagonal brace
description: Plain cylindrical pole whose crossbeam is held by a single strut running a long way down the pole. Surveyed share: São Paulo 46%, Rio de Janeiro 29%, Rio Grande do Sul 23%, Espírito Santo 22%, then a few per cent in Mato Grosso do Sul, Mato Grosso and Minas Gerais. Recorded in no other state.

title: Round pole with one short diagonal brace
description: Plain cylindrical pole whose crossbeam is held by a single short strut meeting the pole just below the beam. Surveyed share: Santa Catarina 26%, Rio Grande do Sul 3%, Minas Gerais 3%. Recorded in no other state.

title: Round pole braced from behind
description: Plain cylindrical pole whose single strut is fixed on the far side of the pole instead of under the beam. Surveyed share: Minas Gerais 30%, Santa Catarina 5%. Recorded in no other state.

title: Top bar sitting square across the middle of the pole
description: The plainest arrangement there is, and the one the community calls the North Sumatra bar: the bar crosses the pole at its middle, insulators spread evenly along it. Found in every state surveyed, so its value is negative — spotting any other arrangement is what narrows the map. Surveyed share: Piauí 100%, Amapá 96%, Goiás 95%, Tocantins 92%, Roraima 91%, Mato Grosso do Sul 87%, above half almost everywhere else, and down to 10% in Minas Gerais.

title: Top bar with two insulators one side and one the other
description: The pole stands off-centre under its bar, leaving two insulators on the longer arm and one on the shorter. Surveyed share: São Paulo 38%, Ceará 26%, Rio Grande do Sul 24%, Rio de Janeiro 16%, Bahia 15%, Mato Grosso do Sul 13%, then under 5% in Paraná, Pernambuco and Goiás. Absent from the North and most of the North-East.

title: Pole holding its top bar at the very end
description: Fully asymmetrical bar: the pole meets it at one extremity and every insulator sits to one side, so the whole assembly reads as an L against the sky. Surveyed share: Sergipe 56%, Espírito Santo and Alagoas 32%, Pernambuco 28%, Rio de Janeiro and Santa Catarina 24%, Paraíba 23%, São Paulo 19%, Mato Grosso 16%, Maranhão, Rio Grande do Norte and Rio Grande do Sul 14%. Unrecorded in Ceará, Piauí, Mato Grosso do Sul, Tocantins, Rondônia, Amazonas, Acre and Amapá.

title: Top bar that looks fully asymmetrical but keeps a stub
description: The pole sits far off-centre, yet not quite at the end: a short stub of bar projects past it, which is what separates this from the fully asymmetrical bar. Surveyed share: Minas Gerais 64%, Santa Catarina 26%, Acre and Amazonas 20%, Espírito Santo 18%, then 3% in Alagoas and Rio de Janeiro. Recorded in no other state.

title: Three uprights in a row above the pole
description: An insulator at each end of the bar and a tall fitting standing above the pole between them, making three uprights that read as a trident against the sky. Surveyed share: Maranhão 36%, Rondônia 35%, Rio Grande do Sul 29%, Paraná 19%, Ceará 13%, Pará 11%, then under 10% in Amazonas, Paraíba, Rio Grande do Norte, Roraima, Sergipe, Rio de Janeiro and Mato Grosso.

title: Top bar braced back into a triangle
description: The arms of the bar are tied back to the pole, the bracing closing a clear triangle on each side. Surveyed share: Minas Gerais 21%, Acre and Rio de Janeiro 14%, Espírito Santo 12%, then under 5% in São Paulo, Rio Grande do Norte, Amazonas, Paraíba, Santa Catarina, Sergipe and Bahia.

title: Crossbeam carried with no diagonal strut
description: Pole whose crossbeam is fixed straight to the pole, with no diagonal strut bracing it from below or behind — the plainest pole top in the country, and one of the sharpest regional splits in Brazil. Surveyed share: Rio Grande do Norte, Sergipe and Ceará 100%, Maranhão and Piauí 97%, Paraíba 92%, Alagoas 81%, Pernambuco 77%, Roraima 67%, Rondônia 53%, Bahia 43%, Pará 31%, Paraná 21%, then 4% or less in Amapá, Amazonas and Santa Catarina. Never recorded in Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Rio Grande do Sul, Mato Grosso do Sul, Mato Grosso, Goiás, Tocantins or Acre.

title: Curved arm bolted onto the pole
description: Lamp arm bolted to the side of the pole, curving up in a long, shallow bend. Common around Cuiabá, Mato Grosso, and around Campo Grande, Mato Grosso do Sul.

title: Astrocaryum vulgare
description: This species of palm is located in the north coast

title: Livramento mango spam
description: In Livramento Bahia, is the biggest cluster of mango production in the entire Brazil. It's easily recognizable with its monoculture in a closed valley.

title: Bactris gasipaes
description: This species, also known as "peach palm", is located in the far Amazonian states, and mostly in Acre/Rondonia

title: Huge bamboos
description: Huge fluffy clusters of bamboos like in the picture are a good clue for eastern Sao Paulo/Parana

title: Calotropis
description: Calotropis or Sodom's apple is found in the northeast

title: Sunflower crops
description: Sunflowers are rare but are cultivated in Brazil. There are three main clusters : western Mato Grosso, southern Goias and western RGDS

title: Attalea maripa
description:
A palm that looks a lot like babassu (indeed it's the same family Attalea) but is recognizable by having a really shorter trunk.
It is found in Amazonia

title: Syagrus oleracea
description: A very useful palm since it's only located in central Goias. It's recognizable by its sad look with leaves pointing downwards.

title: Attalea phalerata
description: This attalea species is easy to recognize with it's extremely tiny and wide trunk. It is found in eastern Brazil.

title: Cavanillesia arborea
description: This tree also called barrigudo looks like a baobab. In Brazil it is located in eastern Bahia.

title: Syagrus Coronata
description: Also called ouricury palm, this palm recognizable by its high and wide crown is located in eastern Bahia.

title: Uncultivated oil palms
description: Those oil palms, that are bigger than those usually found in Indonesia, had time to grow and are thus higher and thinner. Their very dark leaves are still recognizable. They are located in coastal Bahia.
